sections.h2: What a lady bird deed is
sections.html:
A lady bird deed is the popular name for an enhanced life estate deed. It names who inherits a house while the owner keeps full ownership and control for life. The owner can live there, sell the property, and change or revoke the deed at any time. The instrument comes from common law, so no Texas statute spells out its form.

There is also no official form. Sample language shows up in legal publications, and a lawyer should review any version before you sign, because a drafting mistake can have serious consequences. Since the deed names the person who takes the house at death, it can move real property outside probate, the same goal a will pursues through the court.

A seller who holds a house this way faces different questions than an owner with a plain warranty deed. Who has to sign, what the lender thinks and what the county clerk needs on file all depend on the wording of the recorded deed.

sections.h2: Lady bird deed, transfer on death deed and life estate compared
sections.html:
The gaps matter most when a sale is on the table. A statutory transfer on death deed (TODD) falls under Chapter 114 of the Estates Code, the Texas Real Property Transfer on Death Act. A lady bird deed does not.

Lady bird deed and TODD side by side
FeatureLady bird deedTransfer on death deed
Legal basisCommon lawEstates Code Chapter 114
Backup beneficiariesNot allowedAllowed
Mortgage due-on-sale clauseMay sometimes be triggered at the owner's deathNot triggered (Sec. 114.101(5))
Signed under a power of attorneyPossible if the power of attorney authorizes itNot possible (Sec. 114.054)
Warranty of titleGeneral, special or noneNone allowed (Sec. 114.103(d))
Selling and creditor claimsMay be hard to sell without the beneficiary's approvalProperty stays open to estate creditor claims for two years after death (Sec. 114.106)

An ordinary life estate deed is a different animal. The beneficiary gets an interest right away, so the owner generally cannot sell or mortgage without that person's consent, sale proceeds are shared, and the beneficiary's creditors or a divorce court can reach the interest. Those deeds are mostly permanent, while the enhanced version can generally be changed or revoked.

sections.h2: Can I sell a house held under a lady bird deed?
sections.html:
Yes, because the owner keeps full control. The comparison above does warn that a sale can be hard to complete without the beneficiary's approval, so a buyer's closing agent will read the recorded deed first. Have a certified copy ready and expect questions about whether the beneficiary needs to sign.

  • Lender issues. A mortgage may carry a due-on-sale clause that a lady bird deed can trigger at death, so ask the servicer about the loan before relying on the deed.
  • Signature authority. If an agent under a power of attorney signed the deed, the power of attorney itself must have authorized that kind of transfer.
  • Warranty language. A deed can carry a general warranty, a special warranty or none, and the closing agent will see which applies.
  • Recording. The deed has to be signed and acknowledged to be recorded, and it is filed with the county clerk of the county where the property sits (Property Code 12.001(b)).

If you change your mind about who inherits, an enhanced life estate deed can generally be revoked. Do it with a recorded document prepared by a lawyer, not informal notes.

A lady bird deed is sometimes used to shield real property from Medicaid estate recovery claims. It may work in some cases, and whether it works in yours is a question for an elder law attorney.

Texas Health and Human Services runs the Medicaid Estate Recovery Program (MERP). It reaches only long-term care services received after age 55, and only for people who began receiving them after March 1, 2005. Nursing facility care and several waiver programs are covered, such as STAR+PLUS long-term care services and Community Attendant Services. The state never asks for more than it paid, and it weighs debts such as funeral costs and a mortgage before a claim is paid.

  • No claim is made while a spouse is alive, or when there is a child under 21 or a child who is blind or permanently disabled.
  • No claim is made when the estate is worth $15,000 or less or the Medicaid costs are $5,000 or less.
  • An unmarried adult child who lived in the home full time for at least a year before the death can also stop a claim.
  • Heirs may ask for an undue hardship waiver and must provide proof.

For a specific case, the agency's contractor can be reached at 800-641-9356. The agency also looks back up to 60 months at asset transfers made before an application for nursing home or waiver services, so the timing of a deed can matter.

The beneficiary named in the deed takes the house without a probate case, but the county records still have to show it. Practice form books include an affidavit of death used to transfer title under a transfer on death or lady bird deed, and a TODD needs an affidavit of death and a death certificate recorded with the clerk where the property sits. Ask the clerk or a title company which documents they expect for the deed in your file.

When no such deed exists, other paths apply. A will can be probated within four years of death. A muniment of title lets a will prove ownership when the only debts are real estate liens. A small estate affidavit works for estates of $75,000 or less, not counting homestead and exempt property. Texas repealed its inheritance tax effective September 1, 2015.

On the property tax side, a beneficiary who moves into the inherited house applies for a homestead exemption with the appraisal district. An heir not named on a recorded deed gives the district an affidavit of ownership interest, the owner's death certificate and a recent utility bill. School districts must grant $140,000 off the value of a residence homestead, and owners age 65 or older or disabled get an additional $60,000.

Start with a lawyer who handles estate planning, since law libraries will not tell anyone what the law means for their own situation. The Legal Help page on the State Law Library's site lists ways to find one. Law libraries also keep practice forms, among them a lady bird deed form in Texas Estate Planning and another in Davis's Texas Estate Planning Forms.

Two more references are worth handing to the attorney who drafts or reviews your deed: Texas Administrative Code Title 1, Section 358.350 on life estates and remainder interests, and Property Code 5.009 on the duties of a life tenant.

If you inherited a house through one of these deeds and want to sell it, send us the recorded deed and the basic facts. We buy houses as-is, and the closing agent will confirm which documents the county clerk needs before the sale.

faqs.q: Is a lady bird deed legal in Texas?
faqs.a: It is an enhanced life estate deed that rests on common law. No statute defines it, so the wording of the recorded deed controls what it does.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house after signing a lady bird deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The owner can live on the property, sell it, and change or revoke the deed. Expect the buyer's closing agent to read the recorded deed and ask about any mortgage.

faqs.q: Does a lady bird deed avoid probate in Texas?
faqs.a: It can move the house to the named beneficiary outside probate. The beneficiary should still record the paperwork the county clerk requires.

faqs.q: Is there an official Texas form for a lady bird deed?
faqs.a: No. Sample language appears in legal publications, so have a lawyer draft or check the deed.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a lady bird deed and a TODD?
faqs.a: A TODD is created under Chapter 114 of the Estates Code and allows backup beneficiaries. A lady bird deed rests on common law and cannot name alternates, and it may trigger a mortgage due-on-sale clause.
